description:
COSMOS LAB is a multidisciplinary team of five curious minds passionate about astrophysics, planetary science, space exploration and technology. We aim to combine scientific research, creativity and innovation to develop meaningful solutions for the challenges of interplanetary exploration.

Our motto: Explore • Analyse • Innovate.
summary:
Jezero Crater Explorer is an interactive planetary mapping and mission-analysis web platform designed to make NASA’s Mars 2020 Perseverance rover mission data and high-resolution orbital imagery accessible, intuitive, and spatially connected. Built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, the platform bridges the gap between raw planetary data archives and real-time browser-based exploration—empowering students, educators, citizen scientists, and planetary researchers to investigate Jezero Crater’s ancient paleolake and river delta Sol-by-Sol without requiring specialized Geographic Information System (GIS) software or complex scientific data parsers.

Jezero Crater (18.38° N, 77.58° E), located on the western edge of Isidis Planitia, was selected as Perseverance’s landing site because orbital remote sensing revealed a remarkably preserved ancient river delta system rich in clay minerals, olivines, and carbonates—geological environments capable of preserving potential biosignatures from billions of years ago when liquid water flowed across the Martian surface. While NASA collects extraordinary datasets from both orbit and the Martian surface, exploring how a specific rover measurement connects to the broader regional geology remains challenging for everyday users. Jezero Crater Explorer solves this problem by uniting orbital basemaps, rover traverse paths, and normalized instrument observations inside one fast, cohesive visual workspace.
details:
NASA’s Planetary Data System (PDS) and Solar System Treks portals provide open public access to decades of planetary science. However, three practical barriers prevent wider engagement and rapid cross-referencing:

  1. Fragmented Data Portals: High-resolution orbital imagery (such as Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter CTX and HiRISE mosaics) and surface mission products (rover localization telemetry, Mastcam-Z stereo images, and PIXL/SHERLOC mineralogical analyses) are hosted across separate repositories with different coordinate conventions and user interfaces.
  2. Complex Archive Formats: Raw PDS4 data products rely on deeply nested XML label files, specialized binary formats, and multi-layered directory structures that are essential for archival preservation but create steep technical friction for students, hackathon builders, and web applications.
  3. Loss of Spatial Context: Viewing a rover image or mineral spectrum in isolation makes it difficult to understand where the rover was positioned relative to major geological boundaries—such as the transition from the fractured crater floor (Máaz and Séítah formations) onto the sedimentary fan of the Western Delta and the crater rim.

How Jezero Crater Explorer Works

To overcome these barriers, Jezero Crater Explorer uses a decoupled, three-layer architecture that pairs NASA’s live WMTS tile services with a clean, normalized JSON mission dataset:

1. High-Resolution Orbital WMTS Canvas

At the core of the application is an interactive spatial map centered on Jezero Crater (18.38° N, 77.58° E). Using NASA’s Mars Trek RESTful Web Map Tile Service (WMTS) endpoints, the application streams multi-zoom orbital raster mosaics directly into the browser. Users can smoothly pan across the crater basin, zoom in on ancient fluvial channels and deltaic lobes, inspect real-time Martian latitude/longitude coordinates, and orient surface features against regional topography.

2. Perseverance Traverse & Geological Waypoint Layer

Overlaid onto the orbital basemap is Perseverance’s mission traverse polyline alongside curated geological waypoints spanning key mission milestones—from Octavia E. Butler Landing across the crater floor units, up the Western Jezero Delta (including targets such as Wildcat Ridge and Enchanted Lake), and toward the Margin Unit and Crater Rim. Each waypoint marker is indexed by Martian solar day (Sol), elevation, coordinates, and stratigraphic unit, allowing users to trace the rover’s journey chronologically and spatially.

3. Interactive Science Detail Drawer

Clicking any waypoint marker opens a structured Science Detail Drawer designed for clarity and depth without visual clutter. Each waypoint card presents:

  • Mission & Spatial Metadata: Exact Sol number, Martian coordinates (lat/lon), elevation in meters, and mapped geological unit.
  • Visual Context: Curated Mastcam-Z and Navcam surface imagery paired with concise scientific captions explaining the outcrop morphology.
  • Mineralogical & Astrobiological Highlights: Tag-based summaries of key minerals identified by instruments such as PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry) and SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman & Luminescence for Organics & Chemicals)—highlighting signatures like hydrated silica, magnesium carbonate, iron-rich olivine, and sulfates.
  • Mission Context Notes: Plain-language explanations detailing why each stop mattered to Perseverance’s core sampling campaign and Mars Sample Return objectives.
